content: That was {{prev_song}}. Hymns like that one have carried believers through wars, through hard winters, and through long nights just like this one. The words do not wear out, because the truth in them does not wear out.
{{prev_song}}, sung by {{prev_artist}}. Somewhere tonight a grandmother is humming that same melody while she washes a cup at the sink, and heaven is listening.
You just heard {{prev_song}}. I remember standing in a wooden pew as a boy, holding the hymnal with both hands, not knowing yet how much I would need those words one day.
That was {{prev_song}}. A good hymn is a sermon you can carry in your pocket. You can take it to the hospital, to the graveside, or to the kitchen table at three in the morning.
{{prev_song}}. Generations of believers have sung those words, and every one of them found that God was faithful. He will be faithful to you too, friend.
There is something about an old hymn that settles the heart. That was {{prev_song}} from {{prev_artist}}, and I hope it settled yours.
That was {{prev_song}}. Many of us learned hymns before we learned to read. We sang them by heart, and somehow they stayed in our hearts all these years.
{{prev_song}}. When the words of a hymn come back to you in a hard moment, that is no accident. That is the Lord reminding you of what you already know.
I am {{dj_name}}, and that was {{prev_song}}. Some songs entertain us for a season. Hymns like that one walk with us for a lifetime.
That was {{prev_artist}} with {{prev_song}}. Think of all the voices that have sung that hymn before us. One day we will sing it together with them, around the throne.
{{prev_song}}. My grandmother used to sing hymns while she hung the laundry on the line. She never had much, but she had the Lord, and she knew it.
That was {{prev_song}}. A hymn is a prayer set to music, and when we cannot find our own words, the saints who went before us lend us theirs.
You are listening to {{station_name}}, and that was {{prev_song}}. If you are awake and weary tonight, let those words be a soft pillow for your soul.
{{prev_song}}, from {{prev_artist}}. The melody may be old, but the mercy it sings about is new every morning.
That was {{prev_song}}. Little country churches with an out of tune piano have sung that hymn with more joy than any concert hall. God hears the heart, not the pitch.
{{prev_song}}. I believe the truest songs ever written are the ones that point us to Jesus. That one does, and it still does after all these years.
That was {{prev_song}}. Your mother may have sung it over you when you were small. Let it sing over you again tonight.
{{prev_song}}. Hymns were written by ordinary people who met an extraordinary God. That same God is near to you right now.
This is {{dj_name}} on {{station_name}}. That was {{prev_song}}, and it reminds me that the faith once delivered to the saints is still alive and well tonight.
That was {{prev_song}} by {{prev_artist}}. If you sang along quietly just now, you joined a choir that stretches across centuries.
{{prev_song}}. When I was a child, I thought hymns were for old folks. Now I know they are for anyone who has ever needed the Lord, and that is all of us.
That was {{prev_song}}. Some nights you do not need a new idea. You need an old truth, sung slowly, until it sinks deep into your heart.
{{prev_song}}. Hymns have a way of finding us in hospital rooms and late night kitchens. They remind us we are never alone.
That was {{prev_song}}. Picture a congregation on a Sunday evening, windows open, voices drifting out across the fields. That is the sound of a people who trust their God.

{{prev_song}}. Faith is not always a feeling. Sometimes it is simply singing what is true until your heart catches up with your mouth.
This is {{dj_name}}. That was {{prev_song}}, and I hope it brought back a memory of a church, a family, and a God who has never let you go.
That was {{prev_song}}. The world changes its tune every year, but the hymns keep singing the same good news, and it is still good news tonight.
{{prev_song}}. Many believers have sung that hymn through tears and found that by the last verse, the tears had turned to hope.
That was {{prev_song}} from {{prev_artist}}. Hold on to the words you just heard. They have held up countless saints, and they will hold you too.
{{prev_song}}. In the stillness of the night, a hymn feels like a lamp left burning in the window, telling you that someone is waiting for you to come home.

{{prev_song}}. Our parents sang it, their parents sang it, and Lord willing, our children and grandchildren will sing it too.

Horatio Spafford wrote It Is Well With My Soul after his four daughters were lost at sea in eighteen seventy three. His wife survived and sent him a telegram that began, saved alone. Out of that grief came a song of peace that has comforted millions.

When Horatio Spafford sailed to join his grieving wife, he passed near the place where his daughters had drowned. Soon after, he wrote the words of {{prev_song}}. If he could say it is well, by God's grace, so can we.

John Newton, who wrote Amazing Grace, had once been a slave ship captain. After his conversion he became a minister in Olney, England, and wrote this hymn for a New Year's Day service in seventeen seventy three. No one is beyond the reach of grace.

Near the end of his life, John Newton said his memory was nearly gone, but he remembered two things, that he was a great sinner, and that Christ was a great Savior. That is the heart of {{prev_song}}.

Thomas Chisholm wrote Great Is Thy Faithfulness in nineteen twenty three. There was no dramatic tragedy behind it. He simply wanted to thank God for His faithfulness day after day, drawn from Lamentations chapter three. Ordinary days are full of His mercy too.

How Great Thou Art began as a Swedish poem written by pastor Carl Boberg in eighteen eighty five, after he was caught in a thunderstorm and then saw the calm that followed. Creation still preaches the greatness of God.

Blessed Assurance was written by Fanny Crosby in eighteen seventy three. Her friend Phoebe Knapp played a new melody and asked what it said. Fanny, blind from infancy, answered with the words of this hymn. She saw more of heaven than most of us ever will.

To God Be the Glory was written by Fanny Crosby around eighteen seventy five. It was nearly forgotten in America until the Billy Graham crusade in London in nineteen fifty four brought it back, and it has been sung around the world ever since.

Fanny Crosby wrote Pass Me Not, O Gentle Savior after visiting a prison in eighteen sixty eight, where she heard a prisoner cry out, Good Lord, do not pass me by. The Lord never passes by a heart that calls on Him.

A Mighty Fortress Is Our God was written by Martin Luther, the German reformer, around fifteen twenty nine. It is based on Psalm forty six, God is our refuge and strength. Nearly five hundred years later, that fortress still stands.

What a Friend We Have in Jesus was written by Joseph Scriven, an Irishman who moved to Canada. He wrote it around eighteen fifty five to comfort his mother back home in Ireland. He never expected it to be published, yet it has comforted the whole world.

Holy, Holy, Holy was written by Reginald Heber, an English pastor who later became a bishop in India. He wrote it for Trinity Sunday, and it was published after his death in eighteen twenty six. It is a song of pure worship to the triune God.

Be Thou My Vision comes from an ancient Irish poem. It was translated into English by Mary Byrne in nineteen oh five and put into verse by Eleanor Hull a few years later. Believers have prayed those words for many centuries.

Rock of Ages was written by Augustus Toplady, an English minister, and published in seventeen seventy five. Tradition says he found shelter in the cleft of a rock during a storm. Whatever the storm tonight, Christ is our hiding place.

The Old Rugged Cross was written by George Bennard, a Methodist evangelist, and first sung at a revival in Pokagon, Michigan, in nineteen thirteen. He was moved by the suffering of Christ, and that cross has drawn sinners to the Savior ever since.
C. Austin Miles wrote In the Garden in nineteen twelve after reading John chapter twenty, where Mary Magdalene meets the risen Lord outside the empty tomb. Jesus still meets us and calls us by name.

Bill and Gloria Gaither wrote Because He Lives in the early nineteen seventies, during an uncertain time when they were expecting their son. They found courage to face tomorrow in the risen Christ. So can we.

Bill Gaither wrote He Touched Me in the early nineteen sixties. Elvis Presley later recorded it, and his album named He Touched Me won a Grammy award. But the real story is the touch of Jesus that changes a life.

Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee was written by Henry van Dyke in nineteen oh seven, while he was a guest preacher at Williams College in Massachusetts. He set it to the Ode to Joy from Beethoven's Ninth Symphony. The mountains around him inspired his praise.

Crown Him With Many Crowns was first written by Matthew Bridges in eighteen fifty one. Godfrey Thring later added more verses. Together these two men gave us one of the grandest songs about the reigning Christ.

All Hail the Power of Jesus' Name was written by Edward Perronet, an English preacher, around seventeen eighty. In America it is often sung to the tune Coronation, written by Oliver Holden. Let every voice crown Him Lord of all.

Come Thou Fount of Every Blessing was written by Robert Robinson around seventeen fifty eight, when he was only about twenty two years old. He had been converted a few years earlier under the preaching of George Whitefield.
And Can It Be was written by Charles Wesley in seventeen thirty eight, shortly after his conversion. He could hardly believe that Christ would die for him. That same amazing love reaches us tonight.

Charles Wesley wrote O For a Thousand Tongues to Sing in seventeen thirty nine, on the first anniversary of his conversion. It was inspired by a remark from Peter Bohler, who said that if he had a thousand tongues he would praise Christ with all of them.

When I Survey the Wondrous Cross was written by Isaac Watts and published in seventeen oh seven. It is said that Charles Wesley would have given up all his own hymns to have written this one. It calls for our soul, our life, our all.

Just As I Am was written by Charlotte Elliott in eighteen thirty five. She lived with long illness and often felt useless, but she wrote this hymn about coming to Christ without one plea. It became the invitation hymn of the Billy Graham crusades.

Nearer, My God, to Thee was written by Sarah Flower Adams in eighteen forty one. It is based on the story of Jacob at Bethel, who dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven. Even our hardest roads can bring us nearer to God.

Henry Francis Lyte wrote Abide With Me in eighteen forty seven, when he was very ill. He preached his farewell sermon and died just weeks later. As evening falls, he asked the Lord to stay near. That is our prayer tonight too.

Thomas A. Dorsey wrote Precious Lord, Take My Hand in nineteen thirty two, after his wife died in childbirth and their baby son died soon after. Out of the deepest grief came a prayer that has been sung at countless bedsides.

Thomas A. Dorsey wrote There Will Be Peace in the Valley in the late nineteen thirties. Elvis Presley recorded it in nineteen fifty seven. It looks ahead to the day when the lion and the lamb lie down together.

His Eye Is on the Sparrow was written by Civilla Martin in nineteen oh five after visiting a bedridden friend. When asked the secret of her joy, the friend said, His eye is on the sparrow, and I know He watches me.

Civilla Martin also wrote God Will Take Care of You, in nineteen oh four, while she was sick in bed. Her young son reminded her that God would take care of things. Her husband Walter set the words to music that same day.

George Beverly Shea wrote the music for I'd Rather Have Jesus in nineteen thirty two, when he was twenty three. His mother had left the poem by Rhea Miller on the family piano. He chose the Lord over worldly fame, and sang that song for the rest of his life.

Leaning on the Everlasting Arms was written in eighteen eighty seven by Anthony Showalter and Elisha Hoffman. Showalter had received letters from two friends who had lost their wives, and he answered with Deuteronomy, underneath are the everlasting arms.

Trust and Obey grew out of a meeting with D. L. Moody. A young man testified, I am not quite sure, but I am going to trust, and I am going to obey. John Sammis turned those words into a hymn, with music by Daniel Towner.

Standing on the Promises was written by Russell Kelso Carter in eighteen eighty six. He had faced serious illness and learned to stand on God's Word. The promises of God are still a firm place to stand.
Eugene Bartlett wrote Victory in Jesus in nineteen thirty nine, after a stroke had left him weak and unable to travel. It was the last song he wrote. Even in weakness, he sang of victory.

Albert E. Brumley wrote I'll Fly Away and published it in nineteen thirty two. He said the idea came to him while picking cotton on a farm in Oklahoma, humming a popular ballad of the day. It has become one of the most recorded gospel songs ever.

Helen Lemmel wrote Turn Your Eyes Upon Jesus in nineteen twenty two, after reading a tract by missionary Lilias Trotter. The things of earth really do grow strangely dim when we look full in His wonderful face.

Softly and Tenderly was written by Will Thompson of Ohio around eighteen eighty. It is said that evangelist D. L. Moody told Thompson he would rather have written that song than anything he had done in his life. Jesus is still calling, come home.

Robert Lowry wrote Shall We Gather at the River in eighteen sixty four, on a hot summer day in Brooklyn, when sickness was spreading through the city. He thought of the river of life in Revelation, flowing by the throne of God.
Robert Lowry wrote both the words and music of Nothing But the Blood in eighteen seventy six. It asks the simplest question of all, what can wash away my sin, and gives the only answer.

Annie Hawks, a homemaker in Brooklyn, wrote I Need Thee Every Hour in eighteen seventy two while doing her daily chores. Her pastor, Robert Lowry, set it to music. Our need for the Lord is not only in crisis, but every hour.

There Is Power in the Blood was written by Lewis E. Jones in eighteen ninety nine, at a camp meeting in Mountain Lake Park, Maryland. More than a century later, there is still wonder working power in the blood of the Lamb.

Elvina Hall wrote the words of Jesus Paid It All in eighteen sixty five, on the flyleaf of a hymnal during a long sermon at her church in Baltimore. The organist, John Grape, had just written a tune, and the two fit together perfectly.

Judson Van DeVenter wrote I Surrender All in eighteen ninety six. He had trained as an artist and struggled for years over whether to give his life to ministry. When he finally surrendered, he said a new day was ushered into his life.

Adelaide Pollard wrote Have Thine Own Way, Lord in nineteen oh two, after hearing an older woman pray, it does not matter what You bring into our lives, just have Your own way. Like clay in the potter's hand, we can trust His shaping.

Frances Ridley Havergal wrote Take My Life and Let It Be in eighteen seventy four. Later, taking the line about silver and gold to heart, she gave away most of her jewelry to support missions. She lived the hymn she wrote.

Jesus Loves Me first appeared in eighteen sixty in a novel by Anna Bartlett Warner, spoken to comfort a dying child. Two years later William Bradbury wrote the tune and added the chorus. It may be the first hymn most of us ever learned.

Silent Night was first sung on Christmas Eve, eighteen eighteen, in Oberndorf, Austria. Joseph Mohr wrote the words, and Franz Gruber wrote the music, played that night on a guitar. A small village song became a gift to the whole world.

Isaac Watts wrote Joy to the World in seventeen nineteen, based on Psalm ninety eight. It was written to celebrate the reign of Christ, not only His birth, so it is a fitting song any night of the year. The Lord is come.
Jesus Shall Reign was written by Isaac Watts in seventeen nineteen, based on Psalm seventy two. It looks forward to the day when Christ will reign wherever the sun does its successive journeys run.

O Come, O Come, Emmanuel comes from ancient Latin prayers sung in the weeks before Christmas. John Mason Neale translated it into English in eighteen fifty one. It is the longing prayer of all who wait for the Lord.

The words of the Doxology, praise God from whom all blessings flow, were written by Thomas Ken, an English bishop, in sixteen seventy four. They closed the morning and evening hymns he wrote for the students at Winchester College.

Praise to the Lord, the Almighty was written by Joachim Neander, a German teacher and poet, in sixteen eighty, the year he died at only thirty. Catherine Winkworth translated it into English in eighteen sixty three.

Maltbie Babcock, a Presbyterian pastor in New York, loved to walk outdoors and would say he was going out to see his Father's world. After his death in nineteen oh one, his wife published his poem, and it became the hymn This Is My Father's World.

Folliott Pierpoint wrote For the Beauty of the Earth in eighteen sixty four. He was inspired by the beauty of the English countryside in springtime near the city of Bath. Every good gift around us is a reason to give thanks.
Fairest Lord Jesus first appeared in a German songbook in sixteen seventy seven. The author is unknown, but the love for Christ in it is unmistakable. Fair are the meadows, but Jesus is fairer still.

All Creatures of Our God and King is based on the Canticle of the Sun, written by Francis of Assisi in the twelve hundreds. William Draper paraphrased it in English for a children's festival in Leeds, England. All creation still sings alleluia.

Morning Has Broken was written by Eleanor Farjeon in nineteen thirty one, set to an old Scottish Gaelic tune called Bunessan. It became widely known when Cat Stevens recorded it in nineteen seventy one. Every new morning is a gift from God.

What Wondrous Love Is This is an American folk hymn first printed in the early eighteen hundreds and made popular in the shape note songbooks of the South. The author is unknown, but the wonder of Christ's love is known to all who trust Him.

O Sacred Head, Now Wounded comes from a medieval Latin poem. Paul Gerhardt put it into German in sixteen fifty six, and James Alexander translated it into English in eighteen thirty. Johann Sebastian Bach used its tune in his Saint Matthew Passion.

Were You There is an African American spiritual, first published in eighteen ninety nine. It asks us to stand at the foot of the cross and see what Jesus did for us. Sometimes it causes me to tremble.

Swing Low, Sweet Chariot is credited to Wallace Willis, a freedman in the Choctaw Nation in Oklahoma. The Fisk Jubilee Singers carried it around the world in the eighteen seventies. It is a song of longing for our heavenly home.
There Is a Balm in Gilead is an African American spiritual that answers a question asked by the prophet Jeremiah, is there no balm in Gilead? The answer is yes. Jesus heals the sin sick soul.

How Firm a Foundation was first published in seventeen eighty seven in a hymnbook compiled by John Rippon in London. The author was identified only by the letter K. Whoever wrote it, the foundation is God's excellent Word.

My Jesus, I Love Thee was written by William Featherston of Montreal when he was only a teenager. He died at the age of twenty six, but his simple love song to Jesus has outlived him by more than a century.

George Matheson, a Scottish minister who had lost most of his sight, wrote O Love That Wilt Not Let Me Go in eighteen eighty two. He said it was written in a few minutes, on an evening of great personal sorrow. God's love never lets us go.

Stuart Hamblen, a cowboy singer and radio star, wrote It Is No Secret in nineteen fifty after giving his life to Christ. When John Wayne asked him about the change in his life, he said it is no secret what God can do. The Duke told him to write a song about it.

Precious Memories was written by J. B. F. Wright, a Texas songwriter, and published in nineteen twenty five. He wrote it after losing his young son, as memories of home and family flooded his heart. Those sacred memories still linger.
Just a Little Talk With Jesus was written by Cleavant Derricks, an African American pastor and songwriter, and published in nineteen thirty seven. A little talk with Jesus still makes it right.

Wonderful, Merciful Savior was written in nineteen eighty nine by Dawn Rodgers and Eric Wyse. Dawn said the melody came to her during her personal devotions in Nashville, and it seemed to write itself. Each verse honors a person of the Trinity.

Frederick Lehman wrote The Love of God in nineteen seventeen. Its famous third verse, about writing God's love with an ocean of ink, comes from an old poem first written in Aramaic by a Jewish poet named Meir ben Isaac, nearly a thousand years ago.

In the Sweet By and By was written in eighteen sixty eight in Elkhorn, Wisconsin. Joseph Webster was feeling low, and his friend Sanford Bennett told him it would be all right by and by. Within minutes they had a new song.
Louisa Stead wrote Tis So Sweet to Trust in Jesus around eighteen eighty, after her husband drowned trying to save a boy on Long Island. In her loss she learned to take Him at His word.

Joseph Gilmore wrote He Leadeth Me in eighteen sixty two, after leading a Bible study on Psalm twenty three in Philadelphia. His wife sent the poem to a newspaper without telling him. God leads us even when we do not know it.

Beneath the Cross of Jesus was written by Elizabeth Clephane of Scotland, who died young in eighteen sixty nine. It was published a few years after her death. She found in the cross a mighty rock and a home within the weary land.

I Love to Tell the Story came from a long poem about the life of Jesus written by Katherine Hankey, an English woman, in eighteen sixty six while she was recovering from a serious illness. William Doane later set it to music.

Be Still, My Soul was written in German by Katharina von Schlegel in seventeen fifty two. Jane Borthwick translated it into English, and it is sung to the stirring melody of Finlandia by Jean Sibelius. The Lord is on our side.

Immortal, Invisible, God Only Wise was written by Walter Chalmers Smith, a Scottish minister, in eighteen sixty seven. It is based on First Timothy chapter one, and is usually sung to a Welsh tune called Saint Denio.

O Worship the King was written by Robert Grant in eighteen thirty three, based on Psalm one hundred and four. Grant was a member of the British Parliament who wrote hymns in his spare time. He knew who the true King was.

Christ the Lord Is Risen Today was written by Charles Wesley in seventeen thirty nine for the first service at the Foundery Meeting House in London. The alleluias at the end of each line were added later. Alleluia, He is risen indeed.

On Christ the Solid Rock was written by Edward Mote, a cabinetmaker in London, around eighteen thirty four. He later became a pastor. All other ground is sinking sand, but Christ the Rock still holds.

What Child Is This was written by William Chatterton Dix in eighteen sixty five and set to the old English tune Greensleeves. Dix wrote it while recovering from a serious illness. This, this is Christ the King.

The beloved musical setting of The Lord's Prayer was composed by Albert Hay Malotte in nineteen thirty five. The words, of course, were given by Jesus Himself when His disciples asked Him to teach them to pray.
God Be With You Till We Meet Again was written by Jeremiah Rankin in eighteen eighty. He wanted a Christian farewell, knowing that the word goodbye comes from the old blessing, God be with you.

Take the Name of Jesus With You was written by Lydia Baxter in eighteen seventy, while she was confined to bed by long illness. She found in the name of Jesus a joy and comfort that her sickness could not take away.

My Faith Looks Up to Thee was written by Ray Palmer in eighteen thirty, when he was twenty two. Lowell Mason later wrote the tune and told him that he would be best known as the author of this hymn. He was right.

The Church's One Foundation was written by Samuel Stone in eighteen sixty six, during a time of controversy in the church. He wanted to remind believers that Jesus Christ is the one true foundation, and He still is.

Now the Day Is Over was written by Sabine Baring Gould in eighteen sixty five for the children of his parish in Horbury Bridge, England. It is a gentle evening prayer, perfect for this hour of the night.
So ends {{prev_song}}. The kettle has gone quiet, the porch light is on, and the Lord is keeping watch over this sleeping town. You can rest your head now, friend.
Hear how softly {{prev_song}} came to a close? Endings like that are a small picture of how the Lord finishes His work in us. Gently, faithfully, and never in a rush.
{{prev_artist}} has just carried us through {{prev_song}}. If you are a nurse walking a quiet hallway right now, may every step you take tonight be covered in His peace.
Somewhere a trucker is rolling down a dark highway with {{prev_song}} still ringing in the cab. Keep your hands on the wheel, brother. The Lord rides along with you.
Before the next song begins, let {{prev_song}} rest on you a moment longer. This is {{dj_name}}, and I am in no hurry tonight. Neither is the Lord.
A hymn like {{prev_song}} is a candle you can carry from room to room. It does not chase the dark away all at once. It just keeps on shining until morning comes.
Somebody tonight is rocking a baby in a dim nursery, and {{prev_song}} drifted in through the radio on the dresser. Mom, Dad, the Lord sees those tired arms of yours.
Thank you, {{prev_artist}}, for {{prev_song}}. Some voices sound like they have walked through a few valleys. Those are the voices I trust most on a long night.
Nothing in {{prev_song}} needed to be explained. Old truth sung plainly has a way of reaching the heart before the mind ever catches up.
Out past the window the stars are turning slowly, right on schedule. The God who keeps them in order heard every word of {{prev_song}}, and He hears your prayers too.
Caregivers, this one was for you. {{prev_song}} is a reminder that while you watch over someone you love, there is One who watches over you without ever growing weary.
My old pastor used to say you can preach a sermon and forget it by Tuesday, but you hum a hymn for forty years. {{prev_song}} is one worth humming.
With {{prev_song}} still in the air, let me say this to anyone grieving tonight. Tears are not a lack of faith. Jesus wept too, and He weeps with you.
{{prev_song}}, from {{prev_artist}}, here on {{station_name}}. If sleep has been hard to find, do not fight it. Just lie still and let the Lord hold the night for you.
Each verse of {{prev_song}} was like a lamp set on a windowsill, one after another, lighting the way home. Follow that light, friend. It leads straight to Jesus.
Listen to the hush after {{prev_song}}. In the Bible, God often spoke in the stillness rather than the storm. Maybe tonight He has a quiet word for you.
I could listen to {{prev_song}} a hundred times and still find something new in it. That is how it goes with songs that are built on the Word of God.
There goes {{prev_song}}, sung by {{prev_artist}}. Folks who wrote hymns like that rarely became famous. They just wanted the church to sing the truth, and the church did.
Maybe you woke at this hour and could not tell why. Perhaps it was so you would hear {{prev_song}} tonight. The Lord has His reasons, and they are always kind.
It is {{dj_name}} here, still basking in {{prev_song}}. I pulled my old sweater a little tighter and thought, the Lord is good, and the night is not so long after all.
Few things settle a restless mind like {{prev_song}}. Breathe in slowly, breathe out slowly, and remember that the One who made your lungs is right here with you.
{{prev_song}} reminds me of supper dishes drying on the rack and somebody humming in the kitchen. Ordinary moments become holy when there is a hymn in them.
Older saints listening tonight, you have sung {{prev_song}} through more seasons than most of us can count. Thank you for keeping the faith and passing it on.
Night shift workers, the halfway point of your shift is a good time to hear {{prev_song}}. Take a sip of that coffee and know the Lord is clocked in right beside you.
When the house creaks and the clock seems loud, a hymn like {{prev_song}} turns the quiet from lonely to peaceful. You are not alone in that house tonight.
Here on {{station_name}}, we just heard {{prev_song}}. I like to think the moon is listening, too, reflecting a light it never made, the way we reflect His.
Such a gentle way to sing {{prev_song}}. {{prev_artist}} did not rush a single line, and that is a good lesson for the rest of us on a slow night like this.
Every word of {{prev_song}} was once written by a hand holding a pen, maybe late at night like this. God has been meeting people in the small hours for a very long time.
Perhaps {{prev_song}} was sung at a wedding you remember, or a farewell you would rather forget. Either way, the Lord was there, and He is here now.
After {{prev_song}}, I find myself praying for whoever is listening alone. Lord, wrap them up in Your peace and let them feel Your nearness tonight.
{{prev_song}} never goes out of style, because grace never goes out of style. Fashions change, but the cross stands where it has always stood.
Let me tell you, {{prev_song}} has outlived every critic who ever called hymns old fashioned. The truth has a way of outlasting its doubters.
You may have drifted off halfway through {{prev_song}}, and that is perfectly fine. That is part of what we are here for. Sleep well in the Shepherd's care.
Rain on the roof, a quilt on the bed, and {{prev_song}} on the radio. If that is where you are tonight, I would say you are richly blessed.
This is {{dj_name}}. Quietly now, after {{prev_song}}, let me remind you that the Lord does not need you to be strong tonight. He only asks that you lean on Him.
The beauty of {{prev_song}} is that a child can understand it and a scholar can never exhaust it. That is the mark of a song steeped in Scripture.
Snow may be falling where you are, or a warm breeze may be stirring the curtains. Wherever you are, {{prev_song}} found you, and so has the love of God.
Lovely, wasn't it? {{prev_song}} by {{prev_artist}}. Just a voice, a melody, and the truth. Sometimes that is all a weary heart needs.
In the morning there will be emails and errands and bills. For now there is only {{prev_song}}, the quiet, and the Lord. Let tomorrow wait its turn.
Did you notice the way {{prev_song}} keeps pointing away from us and toward Christ? That is the secret of a good hymn, and a good life too.
Truckers, nurses, insomniacs and new parents, {{prev_song}} was for all of you. The night is full of faithful people, and God knows each one by name.
Sitting here at the microphone after {{prev_song}}, I am reminded that I did not earn a single blessing in my life. Every one of them came by grace.
Prayers do not have to be fancy, and neither do hymns. {{prev_song}} proves that plain words, sung honestly, can carry a soul right to the throne of grace.
A friend once told me she keeps {{prev_song}} tucked in her heart like a folded note. On hard days she unfolds it and reads it again. Maybe you could do the same.
{{prev_song}} has faded, but the promise in it has not. God does not grow tired, He does not fall asleep, and He is not finished with you.
Whoever needed {{prev_song}} tonight, I hope it reached you. On {{station_name}}, we simply play the songs and trust the Lord to deliver them to the right hearts.
How many lullabies, how many bedside vigils, how many quiet drives home has {{prev_song}} accompanied? Only heaven keeps that count, and heaven never forgets.
With {{prev_artist}} singing {{prev_song}}, I closed my eyes for a moment and thanked God for the gift of music. It is one of His kindest inventions.
Some nights faith feels strong, and some nights it feels thin as paper. {{prev_song}} reminds us that our hold on God matters less than His hold on us.
Gently now, {{prev_song}} has drawn to a close. If your thoughts are racing, hand them over one at a time. The Lord has room for every one of them.
An old hymn like {{prev_song}} is a bit like a stone path through the garden. Many feet have walked it smooth, and it still leads to the same peaceful place.
Keep the volume low, and let {{prev_song}} linger in the room. This is {{dj_name}} on {{station_name}}, keeping you company until the sky turns gray and gold.
I think the stillness after {{prev_song}} is a kind of amen. No words needed. Just a quiet heart that agrees with what was sung.
For the lonely tonight, {{prev_song}} is a reminder that you belong to a great family of faith. Millions have sung those words, and you are one of us.
Sweet music, that {{prev_song}}. It is the kind of song you could fall asleep to and wake up still believing. May it be so for you tonight.
Morning mercies are on their way, friend. Until they arrive, let {{prev_song}} be your pillow and the promises of God be your blanket.
Steady and true, {{prev_song}} reminds us that God's love does not depend on how well we slept or how much we got done. It is simply His to give.

Beyond the Sunset was born at a dinner table in Winona Lake, Indiana, in nineteen thirty six. Virgil Brock and his wife Blanche were watching the sunset with his blind cousin, Horace Burr, who said that he could see beyond the sunset. Out of that remark came this hymn of heaven.

Doris Akers wrote Sweet, Sweet Spirit in nineteen sixty two, after leading her choir in prayer before a Sunday service in Los Angeles. The prayer ran long because the Spirit was so present, and as they finally walked in, she told them there was a sweet, sweet Spirit in that place.

Charles Weigle was a traveling evangelist who came home one day to find his wife had left him. He sank into years of despair before the Lord drew him back. In nineteen thirty two he wrote No One Ever Cared for Me Like Jesus, a testimony from the far side of heartbreak.

Still, Still With Thee was written by Harriet Beecher Stowe, the same author who gave us Uncle Tom's Cabin. She was known for rising very early, before the house stirred, and this hymn grew from Psalm one thirty nine, where the psalmist says, when I awake, I am still with thee.

Geron Davis was just a teenager when his father, a pastor in Tennessee, asked him to write a song for the first service in their new church building. He finished it the night before, woke his brother and sister early to teach it to them, and the three sang Holy Ground that very morning.

Pastor Elisha Hoffman once visited a deeply troubled woman in his congregation in Lebanon, Pennsylvania. When he urged her to take her burdens to the Lord, her face lit up and she said, yes, I must tell Jesus. He went home and wrote this hymn, published in the early eighteen nineties.

Jim Hill, a Southern gospel tenor who sang with the Golden Keys Quartet, wrote What a Day That Will Be in the nineteen fifties. It has since been sung by more groups than anyone can count, and it still turns our eyes toward the day we see Jesus face to face.
reference: What A Day That Will Be

content: Thy Word was written by Amy Grant and Michael W. Smith, released on her album Straight Ahead in nineteen eighty four. Its chorus comes straight from Psalm one nineteen, verse one hundred five, Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. A good verse for walking in the dark.

Philip Bliss wrote Let the Lower Lights Be Burning after hearing Dwight Moody tell of a ship that wrecked near Cleveland harbor because the lights along the shore had gone out. The great lighthouse belongs to the Lord, Bliss believed, but He trusts us to keep the lower lights burning.

There Is a Fountain was written by William Cowper, the English poet who struggled with deep melancholy much of his life. His friend John Newton, of Amazing Grace fame, walked beside him, and the two published their hymns together in the Olney Hymns. Grace met Cowper in the darkest places.

Charles Wesley wrote Jesus, Lover of My Soul in the seventeen forties, early in the Methodist revival. He wrote thousands of hymns over his lifetime, yet this simple prayer for shelter, hide me, O my Savior, hide, is the one many believers have whispered on their hardest nights.

He Hideth My Soul came from the pen of Fanny Crosby, who lost her sight as an infant yet wrote thousands of hymns. She never considered her blindness a tragedy. She once said the first face she would ever see would be the face of her Savior, and she was content to wait for that.

In Christ Alone was written in two thousand one by Keith Getty and Stuart Townend. Getty wrote the melody and Townend the words, and they set out to tell the whole story of the gospel, from the manger to the cross to the empty tomb, in one hymn that churches could sing for generations.

Stuart Townend wrote How Deep the Father's Love for Us in the mid nineteen nineties, as a quiet meditation on the cross. It has become one of the most beloved modern hymns, sung in churches around the world, because it keeps our eyes fixed on what Christ did for us.

Julia Ward Howe wrote the Battle Hymn of the Republic in eighteen sixty one. She woke in the gray dawn at a hotel in Washington, and the lines came to her so quickly that she wrote them down in the half dark, barely looking at the paper, before going back to sleep.

Katharine Lee Bates, a teacher from Massachusetts, wrote the words to America the Beautiful in eighteen ninety three after standing on the summit of Pikes Peak in Colorado. The view of the plains below stirred her to write about spacious skies and amber waves of grain.

George Frideric Handel wrote the whole of Messiah in about three and a half weeks in the summer of seventeen forty one. It was first performed in Dublin the following spring, to raise money for charity. The Hallelujah Chorus has been lifting hearts toward the King of Kings ever since.

Jesu, Joy of Man's Desiring comes from a church cantata Johann Sebastian Bach composed in Leipzig in the early seventeen hundreds. Bach often wrote the letters S D G at the end of his scores, short for the Latin Soli Deo Gloria, to God alone be the glory.

Handel wrote Zadok the Priest for the coronation of King George the Second in seventeen twenty seven. The words come from the anointing of Solomon in First Kings. It has been sung at every British coronation since then, a reminder that every earthly crown answers to the King above.

Will the Circle Be Unbroken began as a hymn by Ada Habershon with music by Charles Gabriel, published in nineteen seven. Decades later the Carter Family reworked it into the version many of us know, and it has comforted grieving families who long to be together again in glory.

Whispering Hope was written in eighteen sixty eight by Septimus Winner, who published it under the pen name Alice Hawthorne. It became one of the most loved parlor songs of its day, and its gentle duet still sounds like a quiet word of hope spoken at the end of a long day.

El Shaddai was written by Michael Card and John Thompson, and Amy Grant introduced it to the world on her album Age to Age in nineteen eighty two. The song draws on Hebrew names for God from the Old Testament, El Shaddai meaning God Almighty and El Elyon meaning God Most High.

People Need the Lord was written by Greg Nelson and Phill McHugh and made popular by Steve Green in the nineteen eighties. It is a song about looking past the busy faces we pass every day and seeing hearts that are searching for home, the way Jesus saw the crowds.

Find Us Faithful was written by Jon Mohr and recorded by Steve Green in the late nineteen eighties. It draws from Hebrews chapter twelve and the great cloud of witnesses, and it asks that those who come after us would find us faithful when they look back at our lives.

Karen Lafferty wrote Seek Ye First in the early nineteen seventies, after a Bible study on Matthew chapter six. She was a young musician trusting God for her daily needs, and the simple chorus she wrote that night spread around the world through the Jesus movement.

Darlene Zschech wrote Shout to the Lord in the early nineteen nineties during a discouraging season in her life. She sat down at an old piano and poured out her heart to God. The song she wrote that day went on to be sung by congregations all over the world.

Bill and Gloria Gaither wrote Something Beautiful in nineteen seventy one. The song celebrates how God takes the broken pieces of our lives, the confusion and the mistakes, and somehow makes something beautiful from them. He is still doing that tonight.

There's Something About That Name was written by Bill and Gloria Gaither in nineteen seventy. Gloria wrote the spoken words that often accompany it, reflecting on how kingdoms rise and fall, but the name of Jesus outlasts them all. It is a name worth whispering in the night.

Bill Gaither wrote The Longer I Serve Him in the mid nineteen sixties. It is the testimony of a believer who has walked with the Lord for many years and discovered that the road does not grow dull. It only grows sweeter, because Jesus is more wonderful than we first knew.

Bart Millard of MercyMe wrote I Can Only Imagine after the death of his father, who had been transformed by the Lord in his final years. The phrase I can only imagine had been scribbled in Bart's notebooks for years before the song finally came together in a matter of minutes.

Ira Stanphill wrote Mansion Over the Hilltop in nineteen forty nine. Stanphill was a pastor and songwriter who also gave us Room at the Cross and I Know Who Holds Tomorrow. This one reminds us that whatever we lack here, a home is being prepared for us there.

Andrae Crouch wrote Through It All in the early nineteen seventies. Crouch grew up in his father's church in California, and this song reflects lessons learned through hardship. He had seen many tears, he wrote, and through every trial he learned to trust in Jesus and in God.

Henry Francis Lyte wrote Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven in eighteen thirty four, as a paraphrase of Psalm one hundred three. Lyte, a pastor in a fishing village in Devon, is also the author of Abide With Me. This hymn was sung at the wedding of Princess Elizabeth in nineteen forty seven.

Eternal Father, Strong to Save was written in eighteen sixty by William Whiting, an English schoolmaster in Winchester. It became known as the Navy Hymn, and it is still sung as a prayer for all who travel through storms, on the water or otherwise.

Breathe on Me, Breath of God was written by Edwin Hatch, an English scholar and clergyman, in the late eighteen seventies. For all his learning, he left us a very simple prayer, asking the Spirit of God to fill us with life anew, until our hearts are wholly His.

Ten Thousand Reasons was written by Matt Redman and Jonas Myrin, and it is drawn from Psalm one hundred three, Bless the Lord, O my soul. It walks through a whole lifetime, from the sun coming up in the morning to the end of our days, giving God praise at every step.

Angels We Have Heard on High comes from an old French carol, sung for generations in the countryside of France. It was translated into English in eighteen sixty two by James Chadwick, and its long, rolling Gloria has been echoing through churches every Christmas since.

All People That on Earth Do Dwell is one of the oldest hymns in English still sung today. William Kethe wrote the words around fifteen sixty one, based on Psalm one hundred, and the tune, called Old Hundredth, came from the Genevan Psalter. Believers have sung it for over four centuries.

This Laudate Dominum comes from Mozart's Solemn Vespers, composed in Salzburg in seventeen eighty. The words are Psalm one hundred seventeen in Latin, the shortest psalm in the Bible, calling all nations to praise the Lord, for His merciful kindness is great toward us.

Let There Be Peace on Earth was written in nineteen fifty five by the husband and wife team of Jill Jackson and Sy Miller. Jill wrote the words after a dark time in her own life, when she found that peace with God had to begin quietly, in her own heart, before it could reach anyone else.
reference: Let There Be Peace On Earth

content: Charles Wesley wrote Come, Thou Long Expected Jesus in seventeen forty four. It is a prayer of longing, written for the season of waiting before Christmas, asking the Savior to set His people free. On long nights, it reminds us that waiting on the Lord is never wasted.

Children of the Heavenly Father was written by Lina Sandell, a beloved Swedish hymn writer of the eighteen hundreds. She wrote hundreds of hymns, and this gentle one about God's children resting safely in His care has been a favorite in Swedish churches and homes for generations.
